titre: Fifteen Hours of Work a Week
accroche: Among the !Kung of the Kalahari, a study from the 1960s puts the workweek needed to feed oneself at fifteen hours.
contenu_vulgarise:
In the mid-1960s, the anthropologist Richard Lee settled in the Kalahari Desert, at the Dobe camp, in order to count, quite literally, the working time of the !Kung San. Every day, he noted how many adults set out to look for food, how many hours they spent on it, and what they brought back. The received wisdom of the time held that hunter-gatherers lived on the brink of starvation, busy from morning to night wresting their subsistence from a hostile environment. The arid Kalahari seemed the ideal place to test it.

## Two hours and nine minutes a day

Lee's figures say the opposite. To feed themselves, an adult at the Dobe camp works on average two hours and nine minutes a day, or about fifteen hours a week, two and a half days out of seven. Over the period observed, 35% of adults simply do not work at all. The rest of the time is spent on other things: sleeping, visiting other camps, playing, talking. The anthropologist Marshall Sahlins took up these data in 1966, at a symposium in Chicago, then developed them in 1972 in his book Stone Age Economics, under a deliberately provocative title: “The Original Affluent Society.”

## Abundance without accumulation

Sahlins's thesis shifts the question. A society is not rich because it produces a lot. It is rich because it satisfies its needs with little effort, and the !Kung, according to Lee, do not have unlimited needs to fill. They do not store, they do not hoard, and they find the idea of working more than necessary for the next day absurd. Abundance, in this reading, has less to do with what one owns than with the gap between what one desires and what one gets. It inverts the reasoning of classical economics, for which human needs are by nature unlimited and means always scarce.

The thesis has since sparked a debate that is not closed. Some researchers, including the anthropologist David Kaplan in 2000, have argued that Lee's initial calculation counted only the hunting and gathering themselves, not the time spent afterward preparing, transporting, or cooking what had been brought back, which would noticeably lengthen the real workweek. Other ethnographies carried out later in the same region have also documented episodes of food shortage among the !Kung, far from the image of permanent abundance. The figure of fifteen hours remains true for what it measures; what it does not measure continues to divide the discipline.

carte.punch: Fifteen hours of work a week on average, among the !Kung of Dobe.
carte.idee: In the 1960s, the anthropologist Richard Lee put the average workweek of the !Kung of the Kalahari, for feeding themselves, at fifteen hours. Marshall Sahlins drew from it a thesis that inverts received wisdom: abundance comes from the modesty of needs, not from the volume produced.

quiz.question: According to Sahlins's thesis, what makes a society “affluent”?
choix: The gap between its members' desires and what they obtain, not the volume produced
The volume of goods it produces and keeps in reserve
The number of hours each of its members devotes to work
The amount of food stored up in anticipation of periods of shortage
quiz.explication: Sahlins overturns the usual definition of wealth: a society is affluent if it easily satisfies its needs, even while producing little, not if it accumulates a lot, works more, or builds up reserves.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do Richard Lee's figures show about working time at the Dobe camp?
choix: An adult there works on average eight hours a day, as in a factory
An adult there works on average two hours and nine minutes a day
Women there work twice as much as men
Work stops completely during the dry season
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Lee puts the work needed to feed oneself at two hours and nine minutes a day on average, or about fifteen hours a week.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do Lee's data reveal about the share of adults who do not work at all, over the period observed?
choix: No adult stays idle; everyone takes part every day
Only children and the elderly do not work
35% of adults do not work at all
Half of adults work only in summer
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Over the period Lee observed, 35% of the adults at the Dobe camp simply do not work.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What criticism does the anthropologist David Kaplan level in 2000 at Richard Lee's initial calculation?
choix: It rests on data falsified by Lee himself
It counts only children, never adults
It greatly overestimates the number of hours actually worked
It excludes the time spent preparing, transporting, and cooking food
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Kaplan argues that Lee's calculation counted only the hunting and gathering themselves, not the preparation that follows.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where and when does Marshall Sahlins first present his thesis of the original affluent society?
choix: In a speech to the United Nations, in 1972
At a press conference in the Kalahari, in 1965
At a symposium in Chicago, in 1966
In a posthumously published article, in 1980
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Sahlins took up Lee's data at a symposium in Chicago in 1966, before developing them in 1972 in Stone Age Economics.
